# DNA is the hereditary material (double helix) (`dna_structure`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/biology.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Life sciences (`biology`)
- Deps: needs heredity_genetics, cell_theory, atomic_theory; helped by xrays, microorganisms
- Core idea: Cellular genes are stretches of DNA. In plants and animals most DNA is in the nucleus; bacteria have DNA but no nucleus. The thread is two strands wound round each other, with sugar and phosphate on the outside and four kinds of bases (A, T, G, C) on the inside, where A always pairs with T and G with C. Each strand therefore fixes the other: to copy a gene the strands part and each builds a new partner. The order of the bases is a code that spells out the order of building blocks in proteins, three bases per block. The evidence in order: DNA from dead virulent bacteria transforms harmless ones (1944); A equals T and G equals C in double-stranded DNA; X-ray patterns of DNA fibres show a helix.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying Watson and Crick discovered DNA; it was isolated in 1869 and shown to carry heredity in 1944
  - Leaving out Rosalind Franklin's and Maurice Wilkins's X-ray data, on which the model rested
  - Putting the bases on the outside or three strands, the errors Pauling and the first Watson–Crick model made
  - In 1947, asserting it as known: most biologists then still thought genes were proteins
  - Speaking of one gene for each trait or of DNA as a simple blueprint
- History: europe: 1869 – Miescher isolates 'nuclein' in Tübingen; 1928 Griffith's transforming principle; 1952 Franklin and Gosling's X-ray photographs (London); 1953 Watson and Crick's model (Cambridge); americas: 1944 – Avery, MacLeod and McCarty show the transforming principle is DNA; 1950 Chargaff's base ratios; 1952 Hershey and Chase; 1958 Meselson and Stahl confirm the copying mechanism; 1961–1966 genetic code solved
- Read:
  - Oswald T. Avery, Colin M. MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty, Studies on the chemical nature of the substance inducing transformation of pneumococcal types, Journal of Experimental Medicine (1944)
  - James D. Watson and Francis H. C. Crick, Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid, Nature (1953)
  - Horace Freeland Judson, The Eighth Day of Creation (1979)
